questions.q: Why can a form with many active UI Policies accumulate real, measurable load delay, even though a single UI Policy is cheap to evaluate?
options: Every active UI Policy's condition gets evaluated on every form load, and the sum of many small checks adds up
UI Policies only evaluate once per day, regardless of how many a form has
Having more than five UI Policies on a form is technically blocked by the platform
UI Policies are evaluated only when the record is saved, never on load
questions.explain: Each policy's condition check is individually small, but a form that has accumulated dozens over time pays that cost repeatedly, every single load.

questions.q: What makes a UI Policy with "Run scripts" enabled a bigger performance risk than a purely declarative one?
options: It lets the policy execute real client-side JavaScript in its onCondition function, which can do meaningfully more work than a simple field-state change
"Run scripts" policies are always disabled by default and rarely used
It has no effect on form-load performance at all
It replaces the need for any other UI Policy on the form
questions.explain: An expensive onCondition script — loops, synchronous GlideRecord calls, heavy DOM work — runs on the critical path of the form becoming usable, unlike a simple declarative state change.

questions.q: What should a real diagnostic review of a slow form's UI Policies actually look for?
options: Policies that are no longer needed, duplicate another policy's logic, or run expensive scripts that could be simplified
The exact pixel dimensions of the form's layout
Whether the form has a custom logo
The number of related lists only, ignoring UI Policies entirely
questions.explain: The review is about finding redundant, deprecated, or unnecessarily expensive policies — not about rewriting clever new logic.

questions.q: What real-world pattern leads to UI-Policy overload on a form over time?
options: Each new requirement tends to add one more policy rather than revisiting whether an existing one could be extended or retired
UI Policies automatically delete themselves after one year
ServiceNow limits every form to exactly three UI Policies, so overload is rare
Overload only happens immediately after a platform upgrade
questions.explain: Incremental customization without periodic cleanup is exactly how a form ends up with dozens of small, overlapping policies.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what should happen before reviewing a form's UI Policies for performance issues?
options: The Slow Request Log should already have confirmed that form is genuinely, measurably slow — not just rumored to be slow
The form should be deleted and rebuilt from scratch
All UI Policies on the form should be disabled first, with no review at all
Nothing — UI Policy review should never depend on any other diagnostic step
questions.explain: This diagnosis step follows directly from Lesson 1: confirm the problem is real and measurable before investigating a specific likely cause.
